questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of a range-sum query on a segment tree over an array of n elements?
questions.explanation: Any range decomposes into O(log n) canonical segments covered by tree nodes. Both queries and point updates therefore run in logarithmic time, unlike a static prefix-sum array that cannot update cheaply.

questions.prompt: A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) supports which pair of operations in O(log n)?

options.text: Insertion and deletion of arbitrary keys
Range minimum query and range assignment
Prefix sum query and point update

questions.explanation: A BIT maintains prefix sums using the low-bit trick to walk O(log n) responsible nodes per operation. It is more compact and simpler than a segment tree but supports fewer query types.

questions.prompt: What does path compression do in a union-find (disjoint set) structure?

options.text: It sorts the elements within a set
It merges two sets by comparing their sizes
It re-points nodes on a find path directly to the root, flattening the tree

questions.explanation: During find, each visited node is attached straight to the root, so later finds on those nodes are nearly constant time. Combined with union by rank it gives near-constant amortised cost.

questions.prompt: Union by rank (or size) attaches the:

options.text: Larger element under the smaller element
Shorter tree under the taller tree's root
Two roots into a linked list
Taller tree under the shorter tree's root

questions.explanation: Hanging the smaller tree under the larger root keeps the combined tree from growing taller than necessary, bounding height and keeping find fast.

questions.prompt: What is the amortised time per operation for union-find with both path compression and union by rank?

options.text: Nearly constant — the inverse Ackermann function of n

questions.explanation: The combined optimisations yield O(alpha(n)) amortised, where the inverse Ackermann function is at most 4 for any conceivable input. This is effectively constant in practice.

questions.prompt: What is lazy propagation in a segment tree used for?

options.text: Compressing the tree to save memory
Sorting the underlying array before building the tree
Deferring range updates to children until they are actually needed, keeping range updates O(log n)

questions.explanation: Without lazy propagation a range update could touch O(n) leaves. Storing a pending update at a covering node and pushing it down only when that subtree is later visited keeps range updates logarithmic.

questions.prompt: What is the space complexity of a segment tree built over an array of n elements?
questions.explanation: A segment tree has n leaves and about n internal nodes, so roughly 2n to 4n nodes in an array implementation — linear space. Its build time is likewise O(n).

questions.prompt: Which classic algorithm relies on a union-find structure?
questions.explanation: Kruskal's adds edges in increasing weight, using find to test whether an edge's endpoints are already connected and union to merge components. This cycle check is exactly what disjoint-set supports.

questions.prompt: In a Fenwick tree, how is the next index to update reached from index i?

options.text: Add the lowest set bit of i, computed as i + (i & -i)

questions.explanation: Updates climb by adding the low bit i & -i, while prefix queries descend by subtracting it. This bit manipulation is what gives the BIT its O(log n) cost and tiny constant factor.

questions.prompt: Compared with a segment tree, a Fenwick tree is preferred when:

options.text: The data must be kept sorted
Range assignment with lazy propagation is required
Only prefix or range sums with point updates are needed

questions.explanation: For invertible aggregates like sums, the BIT is smaller, simpler and faster by a constant factor. Non-invertible queries such as range minimum need the greater generality of a segment tree.
